walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations in Chemistry — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations in Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations in Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁵
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²

mcqs.q: In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid is best described as:
options: A proton donor
A proton acceptor
An electron pair donor
A substance that always contains OH⁻

mcqs.q: Is relative atomic mass always a whole number?
options: Ar must be a whole number because you cannot have part of a proton or neutron.
No — it is a weighted average over isotopes; chlorine's is 35.5 because of its roughly 3:1 mixture of Cl-35 and Cl-37.
It is CaCl₂ because chlorine atoms are heavier than calcium atoms.
Ar is always exactly double the atomic number.

mcqs.q: Does oxidation only mean gaining oxygen?
options: Oxidation means a substance has been dissolved in acid.
No — the wider definition is loss of electrons, or an increase in oxidation number; many redox reactions involve no oxygen at all.
Ar is always exactly double the atomic number.
Oxidation always means oxygen has been added to the substance.

mcqs.q: Why is calcium chloride CaCl₂ and not CaCl?
options: Ar is always exactly double the atomic number.
Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so two chloride ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge.
It is CaCl₂ because chlorine atoms are heavier than calcium atoms.
Formulae simply pair one atom of each element, so calcium chloride should be CaCl.
